desc:
A non-decreasing array (it may contain repeated values) was rotated to the left by an unknown number of positions. For example, [0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 5, 6] rotated by 4 becomes [2, 5, 6, 0, 0, 1, 2]. The rotation amount can also be 0.

Given the rotated array nums and an integer target, return true if target occurs in nums, otherwise false. Make the search as fast as you can; with duplicates the worst case cannot be better than linear, but typical inputs should take O(log n).
constraints: nums is a non-decreasing array rotated by some amount
hints: Without duplicates you could always tell which half of the middle is sorted. Where exactly do duplicates break that?
If nums[lo] < nums[mid] the left half is sorted; if nums[lo] > nums[mid] the right half is. Only equality leaves things ambiguous.

When nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot tell which side is sorted. Drop one element from each end (the middle already failed to match) and continue; otherwise decide which half is sorted, test if the target lies inside it, and narrow the range.
editorial: After a rotation, at least one of the two halves around mid is always sorted. Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find it: if the left half is sorted and nums[lo] ≤ target < nums[mid], keep the left half; otherwise keep the right. The mirror reasoning applies when the right half is sorted.

Duplicates create one ambiguous case: nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], for instance [1, 1, 1, 3, 1] versus [1, 3, 1, 1, 1]. Here neither half can be ruled out, so shrink the range by one from both ends (the values being equal to nums[mid], which was not the target, makes this safe). That step is what makes the worst case O(n), e.g. an array of all ones with a single different value, but typical inputs still run in O(log n). Space is O(1).
